newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac to take Yeltsin's pulse on NATO.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac to take Yeltsin's pulse on NATO.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac will be the first Western leader to gauge Russian President Boris Yeltsin's recovery from pneumonia, as well as his views on relations with NATO, when he visits Moscow on Sunday.

Yeltsin, who turns 66 on Saturday, is to have lunch with the French leader at a country residence outside the Russian capital, shielded from the gaze of the French media, which has been shut out of the photo sessions.
The Russian president left hospital 10 days ago after a bout of pneumonia, which complicated his convalescence from multiple heart bypass surgery late last year.
Russian television has shown only a brief clip, without sound, of a slimmed-down Yeltsin in his Kremlin office on Tuesday, leaving many question marks over his health.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl met Yeltsin on January 4, just before the Russian leader was taken ill again, and said he was optimistic a solution would be found to Moscow's opposition to NATO plans to admit former communist Central European states.

Since then, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has been to Moscow and opened negotiations with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on closer ties between Russia and the Atlantic Alliance -- although the Kremlin remains hostile to NATO expansion.
French officials said Chirac, after talks with Ukrainian President Leonid Koutchma on Thursday, would give Russian concerns a very sympathetic hearing.

"The president believes that NATO enlargement must go ahead while taking account of Russia's concerns. It is important not to create new divisions in Europe," presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.
While Paris opposes any Russian veto on European security, another official said: "We will plead Russia's case in NATO."

The official said Paris supported Moscow's demands for a binding charter on Russia-NATO relations and felt the United States was still trying to fob off the Russians with a few, non-binding pledges. Washington and most NATO allies oppose a legally binding accord requiring parliamentary ratification.
It was important that European allies play a full part in building the new relationship with Moscow and not just leave the negotiations to Washington and NATO officials, he said.

Chirac will press for a substantial deal between the 16-nation alliance and Russia to be worked out before a planned NATO summit in Madrid in July, but French officials acknowledge that deadline could be missed because of uncertainty in Moscow.

"We may be facing another electoral process in Russia, with the risk of (anti-Western) competition between brown and red nationalists," one Paris official said, referring to concern that there may have to be a new presidential election this year.

Yeltsin cancelled a planned visit to the Netherlands next Monday on doctors' advice to avoid air travel. He had been due to hold talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who currently holds the rotating six-month presidency of the European Union.
French officials said the main elements of a Russia-NATO deal were clear:
-- an enhanced Partnership for Peace arrangement involving military cooperation and crisis consultation mechanisms,

-- a revised treaty on the balance of conventional forces in Europe (the Warsaw Pact was still in force when the first one was signed in 1990) taking account of Russia's security needs, notably in the Caucasus,
-- more financial aid from the West and a full role in the annual Group of Seven summit of major industrial powers,
-- fresh arms control negotiations with the United States to reduce the imbalance in submarine-based nuclear missiles.
